## Forest Above the Volcanoes

Cerro Verde is in the Santa Ana department and forms part of the [Los Volcanes](/el-salvador/place/los-volcanes-national-park/) volcanic complex. Walking trails wind through the trees, with viewpoints in the open areas. From here, the dark cone of Izalco is clearly visible, one of the most recognizable landscapes in western El Salvador.

The "Mysterious Flowers" and "Window to Nature" nature trails offer ways to explore Cerro Verde. The walk passes through forest vegetation, with stops at viewpoints to admire neighboring volcanoes and take photographs.

## A Walk or a Climb

Cerro Verde offers time in the mountains without a mandatory climb to a volcanic crater. A visit focused on viewpoints and a forest walk is less physically demanding than climbing Izalco or Santa Ana. If trekking is your goal, its route and guiding arrangements are agreed separately.

## Cerro Verde on an Ada Tours Itinerary

On the [Best of El Salvador](/el-salvador/tour/el-salvador-san-salvador-suchitoto-gulf-of-fonseca/) tour, Cerro Verde is part of the volcanic section of the journey. The route then continues to the [Route of Flowers](/el-salvador/place/ruta-de-las-flores/), where mountain landscapes give way to coffee plantations and small towns.

The Paraguayan Chaco covers the northwestern part of the country. Dry forests and open plains stretch between scattered settlements. Traveling through the region reveals a natural environment that contrasts sharply with the greener, hillier areas of eastern Paraguay.

The Chaco is associated with salt lagoons, conservation centers, and Mennonite colonies. Filadelfia and Neuland are among its towns, while individual historical sites recall the Chaco War. A journey through the region combines wildlife watching with stories of settlers and community life amid the dry forests.
